item.title: Health Professional Licensing Office temporary closure Tuesday
item.description: The Department of Public Health and Social Services will temporarily close its Health Professional Licensing Office from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday. The closure will allow staff to facilitate the National Nurse Aide Assessment Program examinations, which are part of the certification process for individuals seeking to become Certified Nursing Assistants.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services will temporarily close its Health Professional Licensing Office from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday.

The closure will allow staff to facilitate the National Nurse Aide Assessment Program examinations, which are part of the certification process for individuals seeking to become Certified Nursing Assistants.

HPLO services will be unavailable to the public during the closure. Regular office operations will resume at 8 a.m. Wednesday.

For more information, contact HPLO at hplo@dphss.guam.gov or visit guamhplo.org

item.title: Tropical Storm Champi track shifts to the south, passing over Guam
item.description: Tropical Storm Champi’s path has shifted to the south, with the current forecast track taking the storm directly over Guam. However, forecasters caution that the track could still shift.
item.content:encoded:
Tropical Storm Champi’s path has shifted to the south, with the current forecast track taking the storm directly over Guam.

However, forecasters caution that the track could still shift.

Champi is expected to intensify, likely becoming a Category 2 typhoon with winds over 100 mph when it passes through the Marianas this weekend.

As of 4 a.m. Friday, Champi was located at 11.6 degrees north latitude and 156.5 degrees east longitude, or about 800 miles east of Guam. The storm had winds of 40 mph, and it was headed west at 12 mph.

Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan are under a typhoon watch and a flood watch. Forecasters say damaging winds are likely late Saturday night and Sunday.

Residents are advised to pick up loose debris on their property, restock their emergency kits and gather any medications or other essentials in preparation for power outages.

item.title: ‘Do not focus on the exact forecast track’: NWS says widespread damage possible anywhere in Marianas
item.description: Forecasters with the National Weather Service are urging residents to prepare for potential damage as the developing storm approaches the Marianas, and remember the system could still shift direction. “It is vital that you do not focus on the exact forecast track. To do so could result in bad decisions and place you or those you are responsible for at greater risk,” the Weather Service said in a s
item.content:encoded:
Forecasters with the National Weather Service are urging residents to prepare for potential damage as the developing storm approaches the Marianas, and remember the system could still shift direction.

“It is vital that you do not focus on the exact forecast track. To do so could result in bad decisions and place you or those you are responsible for at greater risk,” the Weather Service said in a statement Thursday evening. “It is too early to provide exact wind and surge forecast values for specific locations. A general concern should be for the possibility of at least widespread damage somewhere within Guam and the Northern Marianas.”

Governors of both Guam and the CNMI placed their islands in Condition of Readiness 3 Thursday, and the National Weather Service issued a typhoon watch for Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan.

On Thursday afternoon, the center of TD29 was located near 10.8 north latitude and 158.9 east longitude, about 970 miles east of Guam.

The storm was moving west-northwest at 13 mph. The system is expected to make a turn toward the west over the next couple of days. Storm intensity was 35 mph, and it is expected to begin intensifying Friday.

The storm is expected to pass between Guam and Rota beginning early Sunday morning.

item.title: Hit a midlife wall? This test identifies your strengths and what matters to you
item.description: When's the last time you asked yourself: What do I love to do? What makes me feel alive? Earlier this year, as Ailsa Chang planned her 50th birthday party, I welcomed her to this side of life. Ailsa and I pick up that conversation on All Things Considered as I launch a new podcast, Your Turn with Allison Aubrey , aimed at navigating the twists and turns of midlife.
item.content:encoded:
When's the last time you asked yourself: What do I love to do? What makes me feel alive?

Earlier this year, as Ailsa Chang planned her 50th birthday party, I welcomed her to this side of life. Ailsa and I pick up that conversation on All Things Considered as I launch a new podcast, Your Turn with Allison Aubrey , aimed at navigating the twists and turns of midlife.

If you've been focused on work deadlines and family obligations, without much time to focus on yourself, you're in good company. And in midlife, a lot can shift: Kids launch. Careers and relationships change. These transitions can be tough, but they also open the door to what's next.

So, I went in search of tools to help me find my way. I invite you to join the Your Turn newsletter journey - starting with this survey that ranks your character strengths.

The VIA Character Strengths Survey is a free online questionnaire developed by researchers in positive psychology, the scientific study of what helps people flourish. The question behind it: How do we go from feeling just OK to thriving?

"Character Strengths are the positive parts of your personality that impact how you think, feel and behave," explains the VIA Institute on Character. After you answer a series of questions, the survey rank-orders 24 strengths, from creativity, humor and teamwork to curiosity, bravery and spirituality.

Research suggests that applying your strengths in daily life can help boost wellbeing and reduce stress. And a study of women 50 and older, found those who used a signature strength in a new way, had increased levels of happiness and less depression.

The survey takes about 15 to 20 minutes to complete. You can take it on your own or with a facilitator. I took it at a retreat at the Modern Elder Academy with Christine Carter, Ph.D. , a wellness and lifestyle coach, and a senior fellow at UC Berkeley's Greater Good Science Center.

Carter says there's value in reflecting on the results.

"What I really like people to do is take it and then look at their top strengths and remember how you feel when you're engaging that strength," she told me. "I think that it can be a real compass for the types of intrinsic motivation that we're looking for in finding our purpose."

Carter has an art degree and used to be a painter. Appreciation of beauty and excellence ranks near the top of her list, along with gratitude and zest. When she's absorbed in a work of art or a great piece of writing, she says, she feels part of something bigger than herself.

One of my top strengths is a love of learning, a good match for a career in journalism. I get to learn something new every day.

This happens a lot. Your top strengths can reflect where you've been and how you've been spending your time. The good news: They aren't fixed. "Your character strengths can evolve," Carter says. Shift your focus, or how you spend your time, and your results can shift too.

If you have a half hour this week, take the survey. Then pick one strength you'd like to make more room for, and invite it into your life. You don't need to overhaul your life to start; one small step can set you on a new course.

item.title: Suspicious mailings to election officials, congressional offices under investigation
item.description: Updated October 16, 2026 at 8:36 AM ChST The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are looking into a series of suspicious mailings sent to state election officials and congressional offices. Officials say some of the mailings contained a powdery white substance.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 16, 2026 at 8:36 AM ChST

The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are looking into a series of suspicious mailings sent to state election officials and congressional offices. Officials say some of the mailings contained a powdery white substance.

It is not clear who sent the mail, which was sent to election officials in states including Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma as well as congressional offices. According to a statement from Louisiana Secretary of State spokesperson Trey Williams, an employee who opened a letter sent to the office on Tuesday was not injured but was taken to the emergency room as a precaution. Law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.

In a statement to NPR, Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said his office was among those targeted.

"My office is in touch with the FBI, U.S. Postal Service and Senate security officials following a suspicious package the U.S. Postal Service intercepted before reaching our office. Thankfully, no threat was posed to my staff or our office," Padilla said.

"Still, this incident is a stark reminder of the very real dangers facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections in the face of increasingly hostile political rhetoric — especially from Donald Trump," he added.

According to a communication from the Senate's Sergeant at Arms (SAA) to congressional staff and obtained by NPR, law enforcement officials are "working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations."

Deputy Chief Inspector Brendan Donahue of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service says that the organization was able to stop the delivery of at least one of the mailings.

"Some of the letters have contained an unknown substance, and we're working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," Donahue said.

The SAA's note to staff said that all suspicious letters, packages or substances "should be treated as potentially hazardous and handled in accordance with established safety protocols," and warned staff not to handle suspicious letters and leave the area where they are discovered.

The note said the mail could be indicated by discoloration, powder emanating from the envelope and postmarks that do not match the return address. An image included in the communication had a return address labeled "DSA" and a New York City return address.

The U.S. Capitol Police and SAA did not return requests for comment. The FBI said that the organization is "investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices."

"Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the agency said. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters."

The investigation mirrors 2024 incidents in which more than 15 state election offices received suspicious mailings.

Now, with less than three weeks until Nov. 3, voting officials around the country are working to carry out the midterm elections. In a statement, the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said that "those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties."

item.title: U.S. historic preservation law faces the most serious threat in its 60-year history
item.description: It's been exactly 60 years since President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) into law, alongside half a dozen conservation bills. "We have come here this morning to give part of our country back to its people," Johnson declared at the bill signing on Oct. 15, 1966.
item.content:encoded:
It's been exactly 60 years since President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) into law, alongside half a dozen conservation bills.

"We have come here this morning to give part of our country back to its people," Johnson declared at the bill signing on Oct. 15, 1966.

Now, historic preservation advocates say, the government is trying to yank the public's power away.

"Preservation, from its inception, has worked best with public and private partnership," Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation, told NPR. "Over the last year and a half, the federal government has divested that responsibility."

It's a far cry from 1966, when the NHPA created a mechanism for identifying and protecting the country's historic sites — ranging from a single tree to an entire district.

Because of that law, those landmarks — today, more than 100,000 of them — are listed on the official National Register of Historic Places. And federal agencies must consult with states, tribes and stakeholders before beginning any projects that could potentially harm them, through a process called Section 106 review.

"Section 106 is in many ways the teeth behind the National Historic Preservation Act," said Elihu Rubin, a professor of architecture and urban studies at the Yale School of Architecture. "It is Section 106 that insists … that federal projects that threaten historic resources can only proceed when efforts are made to mitigate the impacts on those resources."

Section 106 has saved historic buildings from demolition and prevented development on archaeological sites, according to " success stories " recently compiled by the National Trust for Historic Preservation. But, Rubin stresses, the review process doesn't necessarily stop projects from happening — and that's the point of participating in it.

"Some of the most interesting projects that come out of it are surveys of fascinating buildings or places that will be lost," he said. "But we gain a lot from that process."

That process is now facing dual threats. A federal council packed with Trump appointees voted this summer to weaken Section 106 regulations , while a bipartisan permitting reform bill gaining traction in the Senate would significantly narrow the review process in order to speed up infrastructure and energy projects.

"It will effectively rewrite the National Historic Preservation Act in ways that, for all intents and purposes, gut its meaning and protections for hundreds of thousands of sites across the country," said Greg Werkheiser, whose law firm, Cultural Heritage Partners, is leading a coalition to protect Section 106.

" Section 106 Strong ," which officially launched Thursday, says it spans 1,000 organizations — including religious, environmental and civil rights groups — and Tribal Nations collectively representing more than 9 million Americans.

"I've been involved in historic preservation and politics for 30 years, and I've rarely seen a movement come together this quickly," he told NPR. "I think Americans are simply fed up with watching their history manipulated, defaced, or destroyed as an instrument of political power."

During the Great Depression, the federal government hired workers to survey historic buildings across the U.S. They documented 12,000. But by 1965, when Johnson convened a committee to study the issue, half of those buildings had been either destroyed or damaged beyond repair.

"Folks concluded that if … we don't have some strong federal provisions, the natural instinct to just build as fast as you can, wherever you can, is going to take over," Werkheiser said.

The push for historic preservation was borne out of public backlash to post-World War II urban renewal and highway construction, which displaced entire communities and destroyed many American landmarks — including New York City's original Penn Station .

"Because so much of the funding and impetus from these projects were coming from federal housing policy, there was an idea here that there needed to be a framework put in place to identify historic resources and to — if not protect them entirely — at least to acknowledge them and then to mitigate the negative impacts," Rubin explains.

The 1966 law provided that framework. Among other provisions, it tasked every state with opening its own office to administer national preservation programs.

Native American tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations weren't included in those duties until 1992, one of the last major amendments to the law. Leaders of the Tribal Historic Preservation Officers (NATHPO) told NPR that tribal communities now risk losing the seat at the table that it took them so long to get.

"The changes that are being proposed now — both on the regulatory front and the statutory front — would represent an enormous and devastating setback not just to pre-1992, but to pre-1966 historical preservation and the state of tribal voice and perspectives being considered," said Valerie Grussing, NATHPO's executive director of legislative affairs and strategic partnerships.

Historic preservation experts maintain that Section 106 gives experts and the public visibility into federal construction projects without significantly slowing them down. In fact, the National Trust for Historic Preservation says the nationwide average for a review is 16 days, and that 98% of those reviews conclude that the project will have no adverse effect on nearby historic resources.

"At the end of the day, it's [about] whether or not the federal government can come into your backyard and to your community and do whatever they want," said Chris Cody, senior associate general counsel for the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

These days, Cody estimates that his two-person team spends about 70 hours a week answering calls for help from local jurisdictions while also fighting federal cases in Washington, D.C. For example, the National Trust sued the Trump administration over the construction of its White House ballroom , but lost after the Supreme Court ruled the nonprofit lacked legal standing.

That's one of many of President Trump's controversial renovations — including his proposed arch and municipal golf course redevelopment — that critics say are bulldozing over historic preservation laws and norms. It's against this backdrop that the National Trust for Historic Preservation recently launched a defense fund , aiming to raise an initial $10 million to protect the places and laws now in the crosshairs.

Cody calls this a "moment of existential crisis" for preservation efforts nationwide, not just in D.C.

"There is somewhat of a trickle-down effect happening around the country, as various, I would call them, bad actors are trying to push the limits of the law in regards to historic preservation," Cody said. "It just seems to be a moment in time where everyone … who does not care about preservation or has it sublimated to other goals is trying to push the envelope."

Leggs, who leads the National Trust, said "every American should be concerned" about this trend, not only because it could spell trouble for a church or cemetery of personal significance, but because of the "wisdom, lessons, education and inspiration that is imbued in historic places" — and could be lost — to future generations.

The 1966 law also created the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency tasked with advising Congress and the president on such matters. Twenty of its 24 current members were appointed by Trump.

In July, the council voted to weaken Section 106 regulations in a few notable ways. It would limit what kinds of properties can be considered historic in the first place, excluding "significant landscape features" like the Grand Canyon. The change would also make public comment on new projects optional and remove the requirement to consult with Native American tribes.

Those changes are still going through the federal rulemaking process, which includes a 30-day public comment period that has not yet opened. The council next meets on Nov. 10. In the meantime, another threat to Section 106 has emerged in Congress — one that historic preservation advocates say is even more serious.

item.title: Inside a Chicago home, a photographer documents the life her family built

item.content:encoded:
For eight years, artist Jennifer Teresa Villanueva has photographed the everyday lives of her family, documenting intimate moments of love, care and sacrifice inside their Chicago home. The project began in 2018, after her grandmother was hospitalized, and grew into a personal exploration of the immigrant experience.

NPR asked Villanueva about what inspired the project, the photographs that hold special meaning to her and what she hopes viewers take away from her work.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

What made you decide to start this project, and how long have you been working on it?

It started with my abuelita on March 14, 2018.

It was dawn, and I was leaving Chicago for a four-day trip to New York. Before I leave the house, I always pass by my abuelita's bedroom because it is on the way to the front door. That morning, I looked in to make sure she was safely in bed, but she was not there. I assumed she was staying with my aunt in the suburbs. When I returned four days later, and she still was not home, my parents finally told me she had been in the hospital the entire time.

I was devastated, but also frustrated that no one had told me. I called her immediately, and hearing her voice was a relief. The following day, she was discharged and came home with an oxygen tank that she needed to use while sleeping. She was incredibly weak, but by the next day she was already trying to regain her strength. That determination was something I had seen in her my entire life, but I began to look at it differently after that hospitalization, the first of many to come.

At the time, I was taking a large-format photography class at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. It was my first experience with film photography, and I began bringing the camera into our home. At first, I was photographing my grandmother because I wanted to understand her daily life. To pay attention to the small things I had grown accustomed to overlooking. But the more I photographed her, the more I began seeing my entire family through her.

I began thinking about my mother, who worked 12-hour factory shifts and still found ways to care for everyone. I thought about my father's quiet endurance after long days at the factory, and my younger brother, who was growing up lately unaware of the sacrifices happening around him because he was busy being a kid, playing video games, fútbol with his friends, and studying for the future he imagined for himself.

I then think of myself. As an artist, writer and daughter, but also as the family photographer and archivist. I am interested in what happens when the camera enters a home where everyone already knows one another. There is no distance between photographer and subject. I am photographing the people who raised me, and I am also photographing the home that raised me.

Is there one photograph from this series that feels especially meaningful to you? What's the story behind it?

This is difficult for me because every photograph carries a different memory, but the photograph of my abuelita looking at herself in the mirror is especially close to my heart.

During a visit to Chicago in the winter of 2022, while I was an MFA student at the University of Texas at Austin, I asked my abuelita if she had ever been to the Art Institute of Chicago. She looked at me and said, " No, mija, nunca he ido a un museo de arte ." I immediately took her. I wanted to show her the museum that had shaped so much of my own understanding of art when I was growing up in Chicago.

As we strolled through the Arts of the Americas galleries, we stopped in front of Ellen Emmet Rand's Woman before the Mirror (1925). I was struck by the woman's posture and the confidence in her gaze. She sat before a mirror as if she were completely aware of herself and her place in the room. I looked at the painting, then at my abuelita, and thought: That is her.

As soon as we arrived home, I wanted to re-create the feeling and painting and make it our own. My abuelita was already dressed for bed in satin pajama pants and a black tank top with lace and sequins that caught the fluorescent light in our living room. I moved her rocking chair from her small bedroom into the living room and placed it in front of the mirror. I barely had to direct her. She simply sat down and looked at her reflection.

The photograph is staged, but it is completely truthful. Everything in it belongs to our home: the cracked walls, the chipped paint around the windows, the smudges on the mirror, the old radiator that carried us through brutal Chicago winters. Our lived-in home began to remind me a lot of my abuelita's abandoned home in Monterrey, Nuevo León. Behind her is a painting of a tiger, which almost feels like a reflection of her own fierce independence and unapologetic strength.

There is also a bruise on her right shoulder, near the arm where she receives dialysis. At night, she usually feels most comfortable wearing a tank top and leaving that arm uncovered. During the day, she often hides it beneath sweaters and long sleeves. Seeing that part of her body in the photograph reminded me that her strength has never meant that she is untouched by pain.

My abuelita goes through dialysis three or four times a week, and yet, there she was in front of the mirror, wearing her pearls and sequins, looking radiant and entirely herself. The pearls were a gift from her best friend, Don Emilio, whom she met through dialysis and unfortunately passed away. To her, they represent protection, wisdom and good luck.

I think that is what I wanted to preserve in the photograph. Not an image of illness, but an image of my grandmother looking back at herself and continuing to recognize the woman she has always been.

What has surprised you most while working on this project? Has it changed the way you think about yourself or your family?

What surprised me the most was how supportive my family became when I started carrying a camera around them.

I do not remember having a formal conversation with them about becoming the person who photographs our family. It happened gradually, and collaboratively. I would bring the camera into the kitchen, the living room, the bedroom, the backyard — even, at times, outside around our neighborhood running errands, and even to their workplace.

On the other hand, my father was not comfortable with being photographed at first. He was a private person, and our home is an incredibly vulnerable place to be photographed. Over time, especially during a tragic event, he began to understand that I was not trying to expose him. I was trying to honor him.

A photograph that comes to mind is one I made with a 13-second exposure while my father had fallen asleep watching fútbol. He had just come home from his job as a tool-and-die maker at a factory. His work clothes, lunch box and duffel bag were still there, and the television glowed and cast this luminous green light across the room. It is such an ordinary scene, but I grew up watching that exact routine. Sometimes I think that was one of the few places where I could see him completely let go.

Photography has made me more aware of how much of our family life was communicated through these routines rather than through communication. My mother shows love by working, cooking, sending money to family in Mexico, and making sure everyone has what they need. My father shows love through endurance and providing. My grandmother shows love by continuing to participate in family life even when her body is asking her to slow down.

I also never expected the photographs to travel as far as they have. I am the first person in my family that is an artist, pursuing a college degree, and eventually a master's degree. I have been part of prestigious programs and exhibitions, and now my father tells people that his daughter is an artist. He talks about these things with a pride that I don't think he always knows how to express directly to me.

That means a lot to me. The camera began as a way of paying attention to my family, but it has also become something we share. I think we all slowly realized that our ordinary life was worth remembering and sharing.

What format and equipment did you use to make these photographs, and why did you choose to work that way?

My first introduction to film photography wasn't through a 35mm camera. It was through a 4x5 large-format camera at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. I remember carrying that enormous camera around our small house and trying to find enough space to set it up. I would practically be pressed against the wall. It was frustrating, awkward and completely fascinating to me.

Working with a large-format camera also changed the way I understood photographing my family. Everything took time. I had to set up the camera, compose the image depending on the scene in the house, check the exposure, and then ask someone I loved to remain in place while I worked. I remember asking my grandmother to hold a pose for what felt like 20 minutes. I was always conscious that I did not want her to become uncomfortable, but something about this experience she shared with me made her meditative.
